item.title: Old Drugs, New Hope for Brain Fog and Long COVID Fatigue
item.description:
Brain Fog

Old Drugs, New Hope for Brain Fog and Long COVID Fatigue

Two studies show how repurposed medications may address fatigue and brain fog.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • A drug’s established use does not capture all the biological systems it affects.
  • Fluvoxamine modestly reduced persistent fatigue in adults with long COVID.
  • Prucalopride improved several cognitive measures after depression had remitted.
Source: muntazar mansory / Pixabay

Some of the most disabling symptoms of an illness can also be among the hardest to measure and treat.

A person may no longer meet the criteria for major depression yet still struggle to concentrate, remember information, or think quickly. Someone with long COVID may appear physically recovered while experiencing exhaustion so severe that ordinary work, exercise, or household tasks become overwhelming.

These symptoms are sometimes minimized because they are subjective, invisible, or difficult to capture with standard medical tests. Two recent clinical studies, however, suggest that medications originally developed for very different purposes may help address persistent fatigue and cognitive dysfunction.

One trial found that fluvoxamine, an antidepressant, modestly reduced fatigue in adults with long COVID. Another found that prucalopride, a medication approved for chronic constipation, improved performance on several cognitive tests in people whose depression was in remission.

Neither medication is a proven cure for these conditions. But together, the studies illustrate two important ideas: Recovery is not always complete when the most obvious symptoms improve, and existing medications may have useful effects beyond the conditions named on their labels.

An Antidepressant for Long COVID Fatigue

The REVIVE-TOGETHER trial included 399 adults in Brazil who had experienced persistent fatigue for at least 90 days after a confirmed COVID-19 infection. Participants received fluvoxamine, metformin, or a placebo for 60 days.

Fluvoxamine performed better than placebo in reducing fatigue, with benefits still evident at the 90-day follow-up. Participants also reported improvement on several quality-of-life measures. Metformin, despite previous evidence that it may reduce the risk of developing long COVID when taken during acute infection, did not meaningfully improve established fatigue.

The findings are encouraging, but the average benefit was modest. Fluvoxamine did not eliminate long COVID, and the trial focused primarily on fatigue rather than the condition’s many other possible symptoms.

Fluvoxamine is generally classified as a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, or SSRI. But its potential relevance to long COVID may not depend solely on its effects on mood. It also acts at the sigma-1 receptor, which is involved in cellular stress responses and inflammatory signaling.

However, that does not establish why the medication helped. Long COVID may involve several overlapping mechanisms, including immune dysregulation, autonomic nervous system dysfunction, vascular changes, persistent viral material, and altered energy metabolism. Different patients may therefore experience fatigue for different biological reasons.

It would also be incorrect to interpret the finding as evidence that long COVID fatigue is simply depression. Medications often affect multiple biological systems. A drug’s familiar category does not define every mechanism through which it may act.

A Constipation Drug for Depression Brain Fog

The second study addressed a different but similarly neglected problem: cognitive symptoms that persist after depression has otherwise improved.

Memory difficulties, slowed thinking, impaired attention, and reduced executive functioning can remain even after sadness, hopelessness, and other mood symptoms have subsided. These problems may interfere with employment and daily functioning and may increase vulnerability to future depressive episodes.

Researchers studied prucalopride, a prescription drug approved to treat chronic constipation. The medication stimulates the 5-HT4 serotonin receptor, which is found in both the digestive system and the brain.

Adults with a history of depression were randomly assigned to receive prucalopride or placebo. Participants had been free from a depressive episode for at least six months and had low levels of current depressive symptoms. They took the medication or placebo for approximately one week.

Those receiving prucalopride performed better on a combined measure of non-emotional, or “cold,” cognition. They demonstrated greater accuracy on memory tasks and faster responses on working-memory and processing-speed measures. Prucalopride improved immediate verbal recall and speed on a demanding working-memory task, although it did not improve every test.

Importantly, these changes were largely independent of mood. The medication did not simply make participants less depressed and thereby improve their test performance. The results support the possibility that stimulating the 5-HT4 receptor may directly affect cognitive processes.

Source: Alexandra_Koch / Pixabay

Why the Serotonin System Is More Complicated Than It Sounds

Serotonin is often discussed as though it were one chemical with one purpose. In reality, serotonin communicates through numerous receptor subtypes distributed throughout the brain and body.

Traditional antidepressants generally increase the availability of serotonin across multiple pathways. Prucalopride targets the 5-HT4 receptor more directly. Preclinical and human research suggests that this receptor may influence memory, learning, neuronal plasticity, and communication within brain regions such as the hippocampus.

The prucalopride study raises the possibility that more targeted serotonin-based treatments could address cognition separately from mood. That could be clinically important because cognitive dysfunction does not always improve alongside emotional symptoms.

The connection between the gut and brain is also striking. Prucalopride is prescribed because 5-HT4 receptors stimulate intestinal movement. The same receptor appears capable of affecting memory and information processing in the brain. This demonstrates that receptors can serve very different functions depending on where they are located.

Promising Results With Important Limits

Both studies require cautious interpretation.

The prucalopride trial was small, brief, and designed primarily to explore biological mechanisms rather than establish clinical efficacy. Participants were younger than 40 and predominantly female, white, and highly educated, limiting how broadly the findings can be generalized. Some cognitive tasks showed no meaningful benefit.

The study also did not show that participants felt less cognitively impaired in everyday life. Better performance on laboratory tests is encouraging, but future trials must determine whether treatment improves work, decision-making, social functioning, and other real-world outcomes.

Similarly, the long COVID trial does not establish fluvoxamine as a universal treatment. Researchers still need to determine which patients are most likely to respond, how long treatment should continue, and whether benefits persist.

Both medications also carry potential risks and interactions. Fluvoxamine can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, sleep changes, sexual side effects, withdrawal symptoms, and mania in susceptible individuals. Prucalopride can cause headache, nausea, abdominal symptoms, and diarrhea. Neither should be used for these experimental purposes without medical supervision.

Treating What Remains After “Recovery”

The larger significance of these studies may extend beyond either medication.

Medicine often defines recovery by the disappearance of a primary diagnosis: The infection has passed, or the depressive episode has ended. Patients may define it differently. They want enough energy to work, enough concentration to read, and enough mental clarity to participate fully in their lives.

Fatigue and brain fog are not secondary concerns simply because they are difficult to see. They can be the symptoms that determine whether someone truly feels well again.

item.title: Is It Narcissism or a Superiority Complex?
item.description:
Narcissism

Is It Narcissism or a Superiority Complex?

Differentiating narcissism from superiority complex matters for a better outcome.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Narcissistic personality disorder and a superiority complex share many similarities.
  • Superiority tends to be defensive whereas NPD is more pervasive in a person's life.
  • The treatment and outcomes differ, although there is hope for both if a person is willing to change.
Source: Jerzy Górecki / Pixabay

If you bristle at waiting in line with everyone else, if you feel you know more than your boss with 20 years of experience (and you are just out of college), or if you turn away dates with perfectly acceptable partners, you may have a superiority complex. It is important to note that this is not a clinical diagnosis. It shares some similarities with narcissistic personality disorder (NPD), which is a diagnosis listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), but it differs in some key ways. For a clinician such as myself, this matters a great deal in how we approach and potentially ameliorate each.

What is a superiority complex?

A superiority complex is a psychological construct, a defense. It serves to combat deep feelings of inadequacy. You may have heard of its counterpart: the inferiority complex. Both were coined by the Austrian psychotherapist Alfred Adler, which is fitting because Adler was considered to be “in Freud’s shadow” for much of his life.

How does it differ from narcissistic personality disorder?

As noted, the key distinction is clinical in nature. NPD is a formal mental health diagnosis. Pure narcissism tends to pervade all aspects of a person’s life, contributing to a lack of empathy and a need for validation from others. This is not necessarily the case with a superiority complex. For instance, the sense of superiority may surface only during political arguments or when a person is feeling humiliated or put down.

How do both play out in life?

Let’s pretend a political or philosophical discussion comes up at a dinner party. A narcissist is very invested in gaining the admiration and validation of others. This will prop up his or her sense of self-worth, albeit temporarily. An individual with a superiority complex may, instead, shut down other arguments with disdain. This individual truly believes they know better than you, so they need not bother convincing you. A narcissist may come across as charming and persuasive. The “superior” person may appear unpleasant and arrogant straightaway. Ironically, however, the latter may also be more capable of empathy and understanding in other situations.

Source: Ryan McGuire / Pixabay

The difference in prognosis

As a psychologist, treating both can be a challenge. However, NPD is known to impact nearly all aspects of a person’s life, whereas superiority may surface only intermittently. Generally, NPD is often apparent to many clinicians based on history alone: many job changes with no accountability; unstable, superficial relationships. These individuals also tend to try to impress the therapist, at least initially. Their reasons for seeking therapy in the first place tend to deflect responsibility as well. They may be in a therapist's office only because their spouse, relative, or supervisor strongly recommended it. Those with a superiority complex may present as perfectly reasonable except when their defense is triggered, at which time they may be compelled to act smarter or “better” than the therapist.

The therapeutic process of each

With someone with a superiority complex, it is important to promote self-understanding and self-compassion. Building emotional awareness and resiliency can be useful in helping the individual grow beyond the need to prop themselves up by being superior. As their self-esteem becomes more stable, they can see others as equals without feeling inferior deep down or threatened with inadequacy. Treatment for NPD is generally more complex. In fact, extensive manuals have been written about it. Some of the same strategies are utilized, although there is typically greater emphasis on reducing comparisons and envy. In my experience, many with NPD externalize their difficulties, often blaming others for their problems. Not surprisingly, this is a therapeutic challenge. Still, they may be in psychological distress or, at the very least, confused as to why their greatness is not so easily seen by others. An empathic, supportive approach may help establish the therapeutic alliance necessary to genuinely reach the individual who has spent much of their life relegating others as props for their own ego. A person who uses superiority as a defense may more easily abandon it when other approaches prove just as successful for feeling “good enough” with regard to others and themselves.

item.title: Double Alignment for a Healthy Relationship With AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Double Alignment for a Healthy Relationship With AI

The shift to ensure that we use AI without losing ourselves.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Greater confidence in generative AI has been associated with less critical-thinking effort.
  • "Return on values" widens the picture across purpose, people, prosperity and planet.
  • We must align our actions with the future we want, then align our algorithms with that direction.
Human values, ethical judgment, and artificial capability strengthening each other.
Source: Walther, AI-generated with ChatGPT, 2026

Most humans no longer experience artificial intelligence (AI) as dramatic. What felt like a grand technological revolution in 2022 is gradually becoming a standard asset in our life, labor, and leisure. We ask a chatbot to improve an email, summarize a report, suggest what to buy, or help us prepare for a difficult conversation. At work, an AI tool may rank applicants, score performance, or recommend which customer deserves attention.

Together, these choices begin to shape how we think, decide, and relate to one another. The central question is simple: Does AI strengthen our ability to act well, or gradually make important choices for us?

AI learns from the world we have built

AI systems learn from human language, past decisions, and institutional data. They also absorb the priorities behind those records.

Imagine a customer-service department that says it values care, yet rewards staff mainly for ending calls quickly. An AI assistant trained around that system will probably learn to shorten conversations. It may improve efficiency while leaving customers feeling unheard.

A recruitment tool can repeat old preferences. A learning platform may help students reach answers without ensuring understanding. A recommendation system can discover that outrage keeps people engaged.

The system may be functioning exactly as requested. The deeper issue lies in what people and institutions choose to reward.

This is where ProSocial AI begins: before coding or deployment. It asks whether our stated values are visible in our behavior, incentives, and decisions.

Convenience changes behavior

Human beings naturally conserve effort. AI can free attention for other tasks. The outcome depends on what we hand over.

A 2025 Microsoft Research study of 319 knowledge workers found that greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less critical-thinking effort. It also found that AI moved thinking toward checking information, integrating responses, and supervising the task. AI changes where human judgment is needed. Users require the skill and confidence to occupy that space.

A 2026 study in Scientific Reports offers a related warning. Participants judged whether faces were real or AI-generated while receiving guidance that was correct only half the time. People with more positive attitudes toward AI were more strongly influenced by its advice and became less effective at distinguishing real from synthetic faces. Polished output can make weak advice feel authoritative.

Human oversight therefore requires more than a final approval button. The person must understand the task, notice an error, and feel able to challenge the result. A teacher who cannot explain an automated score cannot defend a student. A manager who no longer understands the process cannot judge whether the outcome makes sense.

Double alignment: get the order right

A healthy relationship with AI requires two alignments.

The first is between aspiration and action. We clarify what we are trying to achieve, then examine whether our behavior supports it.

A school that values independent thought should reward curiosity and reasoning. A company that values well-being should reflect it in workloads and promotion decisions. A public agency that promises fairness should make decisions understandable and open to appeal.

The second alignment is between those clarified aspirations and the algorithm. Once the human purpose is clear and visible in practice, AI can be designed to support it.

When an organization buys an AI system first, people often reshape their goals around what the tool can measure. Teachers teach to the dashboard, employees work for the score, and managers confuse what is countable with what is valuable.

Four questions before using AI

A person, team, or institution can ask four questions:

  1. Pursuit: What human outcome are we trying to improve?
  2. Power: Which part of this task (dis)empowers people?
  3. Proof: How will we know whether the system is helping or harming humans and/or the environment over time?
  4. Prospect: Who benefits, who carries the risk, and what resources does the system consume?

These questions change everyday use. Someone writing a difficult message might first decide what they genuinely want to communicate, then use AI to test tone. A student might attempt a problem before asking AI to identify gaps. A manager could use AI to spot patterns while keeping promotion decisions grounded in evidence and conversation.

Research suggests that structure matters. A 2025 Scientific Reports study involving preservice teachers found positive links between AI use and academic achievement when accompanied by genuinely shared reflection and managed cognitive offloading. Another 2025 experimental study found that AI collaboration improved immediate task performance while sometimes reducing intrinsic motivation and increasing boredom in later solo work. These findings support selective use that protects learning and human engagement.

From return on investment to hybrid return on values

Organizations usually assess AI through return on investment: time saved, costs reduced, and revenue generated. These measures matter. They leave major effects invisible. It is time to shift from treasuring what we can easily measure, toward measuring what we must treasure to build a hybrid future that is pro-people, pro-planet, and pro-potential.

An AI system may save staff hours while weakening expertise, increase sales while encouraging manipulation, or speed recruitment while making applicants feel powerless.

Return on values widens the picture across four areas: purpose, people, prosperity, and planet.

  • Purpose asks whether the system addresses a worthwhile need.
  • People covers agency, dignity, capability, trust, and inclusion.
  • Prosperity examines durable value and how benefits and risks are shared.
  • Planet considers energy, water, hardware, and waste.

The International Energy Agency’s 2025 Energy and AI report and its 2026 update show why the physical footprint of AI belongs in ordinary investment decisions.

This means making important effects visible before a decision and monitoring them after deployment. Consider a company introducing an AI assistant. A conventional assessment might record that employees complete reports 20 percent faster. A return-on-values assessment would also ask whether the reports are better, whether staff retain the relevant expertise, whether junior employees still learn, whether errors create work for colleagues, and whether the system deserves the energy and resources it consumes.

The same logic applies at home. An AI tool may save time when planning a trip or composing a routine message. Using it to settle a disagreement, interpret another person’s motives, or make a major life decision carries a different weight. The more closely a task touches identity, relationships, or responsibility, the more human attention it deserves.

The human choice inside every prompt

ProSocial AI is built through many small choices. Think before prompting. Use AI to widen options while keeping the goal human-led. Check high-stakes claims. Preserve a human route for challenge and appeal. Notice when a skill is weakening through disuse. Ask whether convenience is becoming dependence.

The aim is hybrid intelligence: human values, ethical judgment, and artificial capability strengthening each other. AI brings speed, scale, and pattern recognition. People bring aspiration, context, conscience, and responsibility.

The order remains decisive: Align our actions with the future we want, then align our algorithms with that direction. AI will learn from us. We should give it better patterns to learn from.

item.title: AI and the Wisdom of Uncertainty
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the Wisdom of Uncertainty

Intellectual humility protects judgment and strengthens epistemic resilience.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Access to AI answers reduces willingness to admit "I don't know," even when AI is wrong.
  • Intellectual humility shields against believing AI-generated misinformation.
  • Epistemic resilience—tolerating uncertainty—protects judgment and fosters ethical reflection.
Source: Anthony Tran/Unsplash

New research shows that people with access to AI-generated answers are less willing to admit "I don't know," even when those answers are wrong.

In the study, researchers asked participants very specific, obscure questions about films. Participants could always decline to answer and admit they did not know, suspending judgment instead of guessing. The stakes were raised with a monetary penalty for mistakes. But across every version of the experiment, having access to AI advice nearly eliminated participants' willingness to say they did not know, even though AI advice was usually wrong on these questions.

In another study, researchers found that intellectual humility, the metacognitive awareness of one's own limited knowledge, acted as a protective cognitive filter against AI-generated health misinformation. Participants with higher intellectual humility rated pseudoscientific content as less credible.

The Known Problem of Automation Bias

Longstanding evidence on automation bias illustrates the human tendency to over-rely on and defer to automated outputs. This has been a concern in medical decision-making and other fields like aviation. In the case of AI chatbots, some users may not be aware of their limitations, and may incorrectly perceive and treat automated systems as infallible "like a calculator" or like GPS.

Large language models (LLMs) tend to answer in a fluent, authoritative tone independent of whether the underlying information is reliable. This is highly persuasive, and there is not yet a direct way to gauge the level of certainty behind each answer without independently cross-checking it.

This is further complicated by the fact that LLMs frequently do provide accurate and helpful information and resources, even though the way they arrive at that information fundamentally differs from how humans vet information. This has been termed epistemia (episteme is Greek for knowledge), which Walter Quattrociocchi and colleagues define as "a structural situation in which linguistic plausibility substitutes for epistemic evaluation, producing the feeling of knowing without the labor of judgment."

When Should We Apply Our Judgment?

While reliance on AI for film questions does not have high stakes, it points to larger questions about our deference toward AI-generated information. I am seeing more patients bringing in AI chatbot opinions of their medical and psychological issues. Some of the information is indeed accurate and useful. But some of it does not quite fit their situations, especially where interpersonal or social judgment is involved.

Wharton researchers Shaw and Nave have named this risk of deferring to AI outputs as "cognitive surrender," the concern that people will adopt AI outputs with minimal scrutiny. The trouble is that the devil is in the details.

Applying our own scrutiny and judgment takes effort—and it is not always clear when and how often we should be expending this effort. This challenge is documented in self-driving cars. The levels of driving automation require different degrees of human oversight, and the riskiest zones are the middle levels, where a person is asked to supervise a system that is mostly right and the need to step in is rare. The constant vigilance required and sustained monitoring leads to a decline in attention, typically within 15 to 30 minutes, and cognitive fatigue (”vigilance decrement”) is linked to delayed reaction times.

Valuing Our Capacity for Uncertainty

There is a broader issue with the erosion of our ability to hold uncertainty, a capacity British psychoanalyst Wilfred Bion pointed out as essential, citing poet John Keats's term negative capability, the ability to tolerate uncertainty, mystery, doubt, and frustration without rushing to a premature conclusion or "knowing" (Bion, 1970).

As a therapist, I have found that helping people through some of life's most difficult situations often includes helping them expand their capacity to sit with uncertainty—whether with career, relationship, moral, or existential questions, the anxiety of facing illness, or the inevitable pain of loss and grief. I see this as a form of epistemic resilience—one that is deeply worth cultivating to help us move through difficulty.

The ability to hold space and resist rushing to judgment is also integral for ethical and moral reflection. Ethicist Sylvie Delacroix argues that "productive uncertainty rather than efficient resolution" is essential to the infrastructure of ethical transformation. Prematurely foreclosing ethical questions, which can occur when we overtrust and defer to AI responses, prevents us from holding space for uncertainty. We need this space to make difficult discussions generative.

The Strengths of Epistemic Resilience

In my practice, I am seeing people express immediate relief, excitement, and even thrill at the expedience of LLM answers, which are quick, concrete, and well-defined. Sometimes it echoes the excitement of getting answers from a psychic or astrologer who offers a blueprint for the future. Both can reduce the short-term anxiety of uncertainty but can come at the cost of narrowing one's own imagination and autonomy. Uncertainty is uncomfortable, but it also gives us the capacity for superposition, to hold multiple possibilities at the same time. Our capacity to hold uncertainty allows for an openness toward our unknown future, enhancing our agency and self-determination.

There can also be more insidious relational consequences in automatically deferring to AI. Imagine two partners in the middle of a disagreement over a nuanced quandary. One consults their AI chatbot, asking it to opine. This seems like a neutral third-party, but it is not. This can also result in feelings of betrayal, anger, loss of trust, and disrupt the mutual feeling of being on the same team, by implying there is more trust in AI than in each other. Repeatedly outsourcing to AI can short-circuit growth through communication and conflict resolution.

Nurturing wonder, discomfort, and reflection, without rushing to judgment or conclusions, takes real effort. All this does not mean that we should avoid integrating or relying on helpful AI systems. But in hybrid human-AI systems, it is important to consider not only short-term ease but also the long-term benefits of cultivating our capacity to handle uncertainty and epistemic humility.

item.title: The Allure of Morality in Forming First Impressions
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

The Allure of Morality in Forming First Impressions

When meeting new people, goodness is attractive.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Moral information is used to form and maintain social impressions of others.
  • Morally relevant traits are valued higher and processed more quickly than other traits.
  • People are more likely to attribute positive behavior to character than negative behavior.

Most of us remember the first time we met the important people in our lives: from our boss to our beau to our best friend. First impressions are surprisingly enduring, particularly when they are based on specific positive behaviors or characteristics that we uniquely remember.

We all notice many of the same things initially: physical appearance, clothing, body language, tone of voice, and communication style, to name a few. Yet beyond what we see and hear is what we perceive. We feel chemistry and experience compatibility, often describing a first encounter as incredibly comfortable, “as if we had known each other for years.”

Although there may be many other reasons we are drawn to certain people, due to perceived similarity, resemblance to a loved one in our lives, or good old-fashioned personality “clicking,” there is apparently an additional dimension to the attraction analysis. In addition to the many positive qualities we notice about someone else is another category with deeper, more evolutionary roots: morality.

Source: Thuan Vo/Pixabay

When Forming Impressions, Morality Matters

Savannah Adams and Oscar Ybarra investigated how morality influences first impressions.[i] They acknowledge that moral information is used to form and maintain social impressions and note that previous research on impression formation traditionally focused on communion (warmth) and agency (competence), with communion frequently linked with morality.

In their own research across three studies, Adams and Ybarra had participants evaluate social targets based on their behavior within several different moral domains. When morally relevant character traits such as generosity and kindness were compared with communion traits less related to morality such as agreeableness and sociability, morally relevant traits were weighted more heavily in forming impressions. Adams and Ybarra recognize that morally relevant traits are apparently viewed as having higher priority and are processed more quickly than traits related to agency, suggesting that morality is of unique importance in making social judgments.

Great Expectations: the Power of Positive Behavior

Related to morality research is the tendency to assume “goodness” in likable people we meet, giving them the benefit of the doubt by focusing on positive traits and behaviors. Adams and Ybarra noted this theme as well, reporting that in all three of their studies, participants attributed more positive behaviors to the social targets' character than negative behaviors—in contradiction to research findings that negative information may be more important than positive information in forming impressions. They point out that positive moral behaviors are more significantly linked with social norms than negative behaviors, possibly resulting in “general expectations of decency” from other people.

In some instances, positive expectations of others may turn out to be a self-fulfilling prophecy, as kindness, compassion, and friendliness often prompt reciprocity. In every case, however, although we should always remain situationally aware and careful when interacting with strangers, morality is an important component of impression formation that we notice both overtly and instinctively.

item.title: 7 Parent "Needs" and the Real Needs Behind Them
item.description:
Parenting

7 Parent "Needs" and the Real Needs Behind Them

What parents call needs are usually strategies pointing to something deeper.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • The longing to tidy the house is often a longing for ease, safety, or competence as a parent.
  • Waiting for a partner to notice what you need keeps the need unmet and builds resentment over time.
  • When bedtime drags on, the child's need for connection is almost always what's underneath it.

In the first post in this series, I talked about how what parents call needs are often strategies—one specific way they're hoping a real need will get met. "I need the house under control" points to a need for ease. "I need you to unload the dishwasher" points to a need for support or partnership. When you can name the real need underneath the strategy, more solutions become available and you stop needing everyone else to change before things can get better.

Here are seven things parents commonly call needs, and what's actually underneath each one.

1. "I need everyone to stop talking to me."

Real need: Rest or mental space.

When this shows up, the need for rest and mental space is likely severely depleted. A moment of quiet and solitude can help you re-regulate and reconnect with what you actually value as a parent.

One thing to try: Build a two-minute buffer between one demand and the next. Before the day starts, or before you walk back into the house after work, pause and ask yourself: "How am I doing right now? What is my energy like?" Then adjust what comes next to match your actual capacity rather than the capacity you wish you had.

2. "I need the house to be under control."

Real need: Ease, safety, or competence.

A chaotic environment makes it hard to think and hard to feel steady. Getting things "under control" is one strategy pointing to a need for ease. There's also a social layer: we expect others to judge us by the condition of our homes, and the longing to tidy is sometimes a longing to feel competent as a parent.

One thing to try: Pick one small area—a counter or a table—and focus only on that. The need is for ease, not a perfectly tidy house. One surface under control can shift how the whole environment feels, without requiring anyone else to cooperate.

3. "I just need my child to listen."

Real need: Predictability, collaboration, or competence.

This statement can point to several different needs depending on the moment:

  • Predictability: you want to be able to count on transitions going smoothly.
  • Collaboration: so you’re more on the same team.
  • Competence: you want to feel confident in parenting—that you’re doing this right.

One thing to try: Each of these needs can be met by working to understand your child’s needs, which is why they’re resisting doing what you’re asking. Parent Chrystal’s child would refuse to get dressed every morning. When Chrystal asked why she didn’t want to get dressed, her child said: “Because I like knowing you were the last person to touch my clothes in the morning” (need for connection).

When Chrystal met her child’s need for connection by helping her get dressed, Chrystal’s own needs for predictability, collaboration, and competence in parenting were met too.

4. "I need you to stop fighting with your sibling."

Real need: Peace, ease, harmony, or competence.

Sibling conflict pushes our buttons for different reasons. If we had a difficult relationship with our own siblings, it can bring up old pain. If we have a close sibling relationship, watching our kids fight can feel like something precious being lost. And when we're constantly intervening, our needs for peace and ease take a hit.

One thing to try: A middle path works better than either managing every squabble or leaving children to sort it out alone. When siblings understand why the other is doing something they find irritating—when they can identify each other's needs—they can often find solutions that work for both of them. This is a skill that can be taught and scaffolded over time.

5. "I need you to unload the dishwasher."

Real need: Support, partnership, or shared responsibility.

I once picked a fight with my husband because he didn’t unload the dishwasher. I had needs for support and partnership that I didn’t know how to articulate. Waiting for my partner to notice my needs (or picking fights over wants/strategies) are not very effective ways of getting needs met—and tend to build frustration, anger, and resentment instead.

One thing to try: Ask your partner what's going on for them first. After you've heard them out, they'll be more receptive to hearing about your needs. Then stay open to multiple strategies. My partner could have met my need for support by unloading the dishwasher or by taking our daughter out so I could work, cooking dinner, or going grocery shopping. The need stays the same, but the strategies don't have to.

6. "I need bedtime to stop taking so long."

Real need: Rest, ease, mental space, or self-care.

Parents often feel frustrated when daily routines seem to take forever especially at the end of the day when our capacity is low. And our kids can seem intent on dragging these routines out for as long as humanly possible.

The needs lens helps us to understand why: extra-long routines often happen right before a separation (preschool/school; bedtime), which often points to a need for connection.

One thing to try: Special Time is one of the most powerful tools we have to address attention-seeking behavior in kids. Ten minutes of consistent daily one-on-one time where your child chooses the activity and your phone is out of the room builds enough connection earlier in the day that your child isn't trying to squeeze it out of every bedtime moment. The bedtime routine gets shorter because the underlying need has already been met.

7. "I need to feel normal again."

Real need: Rest or competence.

This one tends to come up in difficult periods—after a new baby, during a challenging stretch with a child, or when burnout has set in. The real need is to feel competent again—to have some part of daily life be manageable and not overwhelming.

One thing to try: Look for something that's going well, even if it's small. How did you make that happen? What strengths did you draw on? The same strengths that worked there are available in the harder situations too.

Final Thoughts

The seven examples in this post are a starting point. But the same reframe works anywhere you find yourself stuck—with your partner, your child, or yourself at the end of a hard day.

In the next post, we'll look at the other side of this equation: seven things children do that parents read as wants, and the needs they're pointing to.

item.title: Choosing the Unknown: Career Decisions in Unfamiliar Fields
item.description:
Career

Choosing the Unknown: Career Decisions in Unfamiliar Fields

Insights into career decision-making when experience and information are limited.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Choosing a career in an unfamiliar field can be challenging.
  • A lack of understanding can discourage people from pursuing certain careers.
  • Exploring unfamiliar fields and learning from trusted networks help people make informed decisions.

Co-authored by Lena Wang, Haiying Kang, Joe Jiang and March To

Choosing a career is not easy; it involves a complex psychological process. People need to figure out their interests, strengths, and skills, and consider how they see themselves in the future (e.g., future work selves), while at times also trying to meet family and social expectations.

Career decisions could be even more challenging when it comes to unfamiliar fields. Without direct exposure, people often lack a clear understanding of what the work actually involves, the skills required, or the day-to-day realities of the role.

In the absence of reliable information, decisions could be shaped by assumptions, stereotypes, or incomplete narratives. As a result, many people may prematurely rule out entire career paths—not because they are unsuitable, but because they are misunderstood. In doing so, they may miss opportunities that could turn out to be well-suited to them and highly rewarding.

Careers in unfamiliar context

Research shows that nursing students hesitate to enter the profession because they have limited first-hand knowledge of what a nursing career actually involves. Exposure to heavy workloads, emotional demands, and workplace challenges during clinical placements often reveals a reality that differs from their initial expectations. Consequently, internships play a critical role in helping students explore career realities, develop realistic expectations, and build the confidence needed to make well-informed career decisions.

When building a career in a culturally unfamiliar environment, people often have limited knowledge of local labour market expectations, employer preferences, and the skills required for success, making it difficult to navigate the job market. To make informed career decisions, they need to develop an understanding of the local context by learning the language, understanding local recruitment practices, and acquiring the knowledge and skills valued by employers.

New study findings

Our recent research surveyed more than 900 university students in STEM disciplines across Australia to explore career preferences and decisions in the national security sector—a sector that is not well known among students and the broader public, yet urgently needs talents with STEM expertise.

We found that students’ career decisions are strongly shaped by their perceptions of the occupation. When a career is perceived as inaccessible, inconsistent with personal values, or poorly understood, students are unlikely to consider it as a viable career option. This is particularly true for careers in the national security sector such as defense, where misconceptions are common.

Consistent with prior research, Gen Z places a strong emphasis on environmental sustainability, ethical conduct, and positive social impact. Therefore, when students associate defense primarily with conflict rather than societal contribution, they are less motivated to pursue this career.

Students also described several common misconceptions. For example, some perceive defense jobs as mainly involving intense physical activities and therefore consider them unsuitable for women. Others worry that entering defense would limit their future career mobility by being “boxed” into a single and highly specialized industry.

As a result, many overlook the breadth of opportunities available within the defense sector, the potential alignment between these careers and their values, and the transferability of skills they could develop.

For example, cybersecurity professionals working in defense protect critical infrastructure, government systems, and communities from cyberattacks and disruptions to essential services. Defense also employs a broad range of healthcare professionals, including doctors and nurses, who not only provide care for military personnel but also essential support to civilian communities during emergencies and natural disasters.

When exploring unfamiliar careers, we further found that stories and experiences shared by family members and peers play an important role in shaping career decisions. Narratives from these trusted social networks are often perceived as concrete, authentic, and relatable, enabling individuals to develop a more realistic understanding of career options and make more informed career decisions.

What can we do as individuals?

Don’t limit your career options to the jobs you already know about. We tend to consider careers that feel familiar and overlook those we know little about. But unfamiliar doesn't mean unsuitable. Challenge yourself to explore industries beyond your comfort zone by speaking with professionals, seeking work experience, or taking on internships in fields you may not previously have considered. Doing so can broaden your career options.

Don’t let stereotypes shape your career choices. Research shows first impressions and common assumptions can result in overlooking careers that may be an excellent fit. Instead, dig deeper. Explore reliable information, ask questions, and talk to people working in the field to gain a more accurate picture of what the job is really like. A better understanding can open doors to opportunities you may never have considered.

Be mindful of who shapes your career decisions. Today, advice comes from everywhere—social media, friends, family, influencers, and online communities. But not all sources are equally reliable. Seek out trusted voices and people with first-hand experience. Their insights, honest stories, and practical advice can help you build a more accurate picture of different careers and make decisions based on evidence rather than assumptions.

Build career self-knowledge. Try to spend more time to understand yourself. Think about what matters most to you, and what kind of work gives you a sense of purpose. Career decisions are often more effective when they align with your personal values, interests, strengths, and aspirations.

item.title: 10 Easy Tips for Difficult Conversations
item.description:
Relationships

10 Easy Tips for Difficult Conversations

Every relationship has conflicts; here’s how to turn them into win-wins.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • The mythic American ideal of relationships without conflict can be a bit tyrannizing.
  • The truth is that all relationships have conflict, whether healthy or not.
  • It’s not conflict that harms relationships, but the way we deal with conflict that makes the difference.
Source: Antonio_Diaz/Getty Images

Every two people are, by definition, different. Even identical twins have conflict. For women especially, the dominant American culture taught many of us to be nice and sublimate our needs to others—whether those others be men, children, friends, partners, or colleagues. Shoving our needs down, we now know, is unhealthy for us, body and mind. But if we haven’t been taught how to have “healthy arguments,” how can we?

These tips are available to anyone and everyone. Try one at a time or many at once; most can be used in any order to help both people in a conflict feel better, and even closer. It doesn’t matter if the disagreement is about parenting, what movie to go to, or how to pick the next city for a move.

Remember, though, “good conflict” is a practice. Just like yoga, jogging, or learning to play a musical instrument, you need to keep expectations light at first, then try and try again, so you work up to conflict symphonies you can feel really good about.

  • W.A.I.T., and strike when the iron is cold. In 12-step programs, WAIT is a slogan meaning, “Why Am I Talking?” When we’re mad, we need to slow down and pause, waiting to talk. For an hour, a good night’s sleep, or however long we need. Trying to have a productive conversation while fuming is close to impossible. Instead, “Strike when the iron is cold.” When everyone has had time to separate from the fire and is cool and calmer, talking can be productive. It might feel urgent to have a tough talk right now, but it hardly ever truly is. The longer you cool down, the likely better the outcome.
  • Talk or listen, but don’t interrupt or be interrupted. This is tough. I myself am the conversation interruptus queen. I am trying. And the longer I keep my mouth shut and wait until the other person finishes talking, the better for all. The other person feels heard, and I hopefully listened and can validate what they said and feel. If they (or I!) keep interrupting? Each time you can say something like, “I’m still talking,” “I’m not done,” or, “Can I please finish?”
Source: SolStock/Getty Images Signature
  • Ask, “Is there more?” If the other person pauses and seems done, but you feel like they have more to say, just ask. They’ll tell you, and they’ll be able to listen to your perspective much more compassionately and deeply if they’ve felt heard and understood.
  • Remind yourself, and say aloud to remind you both, “This is not about who’s right or wrong; it’s about our relationship.” Sometimes, you’ll have to repeat this several times during the conversation to get away from defensiveness, an inclination to “prove” we’re right, or blame. What’s most important to both of you is the connection between you, right? That’s deeper and more worth preserving than accusing whoever was, for instance, canceling plans again, or late to the family party.
  • Validate values—yours and theirs. It’s really about feelings, wants, and needs, not who didn’t do the dishes. You can say, “I value tidiness. My mental space is more calm when I come downstairs to a clean kitchen/living room/bathroom, etc.” Translating upset feelings into values underneath them helps. Whether it’s patience, love, honesty, companionship, or so on, saying, “I value reliability, that’s why I feel frustrated when I heard you say it would get done and it didn’t.” That’s much easier for someone else to swallow than, “You’re just so lazy!”
  • Use I messages and feeling words. Almost every sentence in a conflict can start with “I.” “I feel ignored/disrespected/mad/afraid, and so on. Get out your feeling wheel to help you if you need it. Don’t tell the other person what they did and how mean it was—they’ll get defensive and you’ll both dig in with no progress, only more dispute. Keep the focus on “I” (what you saw, felt, heard), keep the word “you” out of it, and watch listening improve. If you’re the one feeling defensive or blamed, ask the other person to speak in “I” messages to give you both a pause and reset.
  • Apologize for your part. We can all learn to take responsibility for our mistakes. “I’m sorry I yelled at you, that’s on me,” or, “I take responsibility for not checking with you first,” goes a long way. It’s validating to another’s experience when we show up this way, owning our faults and mistakes. Humans make plenty, so embrace yours!
  • Consider family background. Almost always, the other person grew up in a different environment. Maybe they learned they could leave messes for someone else to clean up. Maybe they were taught to do things without asking, to avoid trouble. Perhaps they had to take care of everyone and didn’t learn to consider others’ feelings before automatically moving into action. Whatever their experience was, it can teach you a lot and help you understand where they’re coming from and why. Ask, “What was this like for you when you grew up?” or “What did you learn about this when you were little?” You might be surprised by what they say. That understanding alone can increase compassion and productive outcomes.
  • Manage expectations forward. As the conversation is winding down, you might tell the other person what you learned, or how you would do things differently next time. You can ask them how they might want to behave moving forward, too. Getting through a tough talk is both a personal win for both of you (you’re skilled enough to do this!) and a relationship win. Almost always, people feel proud to complete a successful conflict conversation, and closer to the other person. That’s the goal!
  • Close the deal with, “Are we good?” Or, “Would you like to talk about this again?” Sometimes, “Can I give you a hug?” works. However you want to close, wrap it up on a lighter note. Thank them for joining you in the tough talk trenches. It’s courageous and not everyone can or even wants to go there. You’re both brave and deserve affirmation that you took your relationship a little (or a lot) stronger and deeper.

Keep this list. Any of these tips help pave easier, more successful conversations and stronger connections. Again, almost none of us were taught how to have healthy, productive, tough conversations or disputes, so offer yourself plenty of grace. And your conversation partner who was willing to meet you there, too.
